title: Mel Blanc
description: American voice actor and radio personality (1908–1989)
wiki_lead:
Melvin Jerome Blanc (né Blank ; May 30, 1908 – July 10, 1989) was an American voice actor and radio personality whose career spanned over sixty years. Referred to as "The Man of a Thousand Voices", he is widely regarded as the greatest and most influential voice actor of all time. Blanc provided many voices for Looney Tunes and Merrie Melodies cartoons released by Warner Bros. during the golden age of American animation.
Blanc began his career during the Golden Age of Radio when he provided character voices and vocal sound effects for comedy radio programs, including those of Jack Benny, Abbott and Costello, Burns and Allen, The Great Gildersleeve, Judy Canova and his own short-lived sitcom. He later expanded to animation, providing the voices of Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck, Tweety, Sylvester the Cat, Yosemite Sam, Foghorn Leghorn, Marvin the Martian, Pepé Le Pew, Speedy Gonzales, Wile E. Coyote, the Tasmanian Devil, and numerous other characters from the Looney Tunes and Merrie Melodies theatrical cartoons. Blanc also voiced the characters Porky Pig and Elmer Fudd after replacing their respective original performers, Joe Dougherty and Arthur Q. Bryan, although he occasionally voiced Elmer during Bryan's lifetime as well.
Blanc later voiced characters for Hanna-Barbera's television cartoons, including: Barney Rubble and Dino on The Flintstones, Mr. Spacely on The Jetsons, Secret Squirrel on The Atom Ant/Secret Squirrel Show, the title character of Speed Buggy, and Captain Caveman on Captain Caveman and the Teen Angels and The Flintstone Kids. He was also the voice of Gideon's hiccups in Pinocchio, one of his two appearances at Disney. Blanc was also the voice of Woody Woodpecker in the first four animated shorts from 1940 to 1941, his only appearance at Universal Pictures. He also provided the vocal effects for Tom and Jerry  in the short films from 1963 to 1967, in 34 short films directed by Chuck Jones, and voiced Heathcliff in Heathcliff and the Catillac Cats.

Early life
Blanc was born on May 30, 1908, in San Francisco, California. His birth name was Melvin Jerome Blank, and his Jewish-American parents were Eva Rivka (born Katz) and Frederick Harvey Blank. Blanc's paternal grandparents, Heinrich Sebastian and Katharine (born Schwarzel), immigrated to Brooklyn from Bavaria in 1860 and 1862, respectively. Eva Katz was born in Vilnius, Lithuania, and immigrated to America with her parents, Nolan Chaim and Laura Golemba Katz, as a child. Blanc also had an older brother, Henry Charles Blank.
He grew up in San Francisco's Western Addition neighborhood, and later in Portland, Oregon, where he attended Lincoln High School. He had an early fondness for voices and dialect, which he began practicing at the age of 10. He claimed that he changed the spelling of his name when he was 16, from Blank to Blanc, because a teacher told him that he would amount to nothing and be like his name, a "blank". grok_lead: Mel Blanc (born Melvin Jerome Blank; May 30, 1908 â July 10, 1989) was an American voice actor, comedian, singer, and radio personality, best known for providing the voices of numerous iconic animated characters, including Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck, Porky Pig, Tweety Bird, Sylvester the Cat, and the Road Runner for Warner Bros. Looney Tunes and Merrie Melodies cartoons, as well as Barney Rubble and Dino in the Hanna-Barbera series The Flintstones. Over his six-decade career, Blanc voiced nearly 400 distinct characters in more than 3,000 animated shorts and features, becoming the first voice artist to receive on-screen credits for his work in cartoons. Born in San Francisco, California, to Frederick and Eva Katz Blanc, who managed a women's clothing business, Blanc grew up in Portland, Oregon, where he studied music and began his entertainment career as a musician playing bass, violin, and sousaphone while hosting a local radio comedy show called Cobwebs and Nuts. In 1933, he married Estelle Rosenbaum, with whom he had a son, Noel, and relocated to Los Angeles to join Leon Schlesinger Productions, where he quickly became indispensable to the animation industry by developing versatile vocal characterizations that brought characters to life with humor and distinct personalities. Beyond animation, Blanc contributed to radio programs like The Jack Benny Program, where he played multiple roles including the hapless Professor LeBlanc and Sy the Mexican, and later extended his talents to television, commercials, and even hit novelty records such as "I Tawt I Taw a Puddy Tat" and " The Woody Woodpecker Song," each selling over two million copies. Blanc's innovative approach to voice acting âoften performing up to 20 characters per recording sessionârevolutionized the field, influencing generations of performers and earning him accolades such as the United Jewish Welfare Fund's Man of the Year award, the Show Business Shrine Club's Life Achievement Award, and a 1984 honor from the Smithsonian Institution for his contributions to American culture. He co-produced The Bugs Bunny Show in the 1960s, helping to popularize classic Looney Tunes shorts on television, and continued working until shortly before his death from heart disease and emphysema at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles at age 81.
